source_read: PMC HTML, PMC9974873 (author manuscript of J Affect Disord 2023;326:105-110), read in full in my own browser tab with get_page_text (the whole article fitted in one read): abstract, untitled introduction, Materials and Methods, Results with Tables 1-4 and their notes, Discussion, Conclusion, funding, footnotes and references. The online supplement (Supplemental Tables 1-3, recruitment materials, response lists) was not read.

claims.overstatement: The Simonsson part is worded as what it is (tick-box answers about one recalled experience, untested). One error of order: the claim lists changing the music (99, 16.2%) among the most ticked and then says 'fewer ticked' smoking cannabis, but cannabis was ticked by 113 (18.4%), more than changing the music; the paper's own Results name smoking cannabis, not music, as the fifth most common helpful intervention. 'Fewer' holds only for alcohol (54, 8.8%) and another drug (22, 3.6%). Whether 'two independent surveys agree' cannot be judged from this source alone: its list (calm the mind, change location, ask a friend, change the people, cannabis, music) is a different, shorter list from Wood et al.'s, and the paper compares itself only with Carbonaro et al. (2016).
claims.note: Recomputed from Table 2 (n = 613): 257 = 41.9%, 168 = 27.4%, 124 = 20.2% (twice), 99 = 16.2%, 113 = 18.4%, 54 = 8.8%, 22 = 3.6%; all match. Not mentioned in the claim: changing the environment in another way 77 (12.6%) and using the body to shift the experience 48 (7.8%). All 613, including the 362 who answered 'never' to the frequency item, were asked to rate their most challenging experience and then tick the helpful list, so the '362' wording is right. The Discussion goes on to suggest mindfulness-type exercises as preparation, which the cross-sectional data cannot test.

anchors.extracted: Of 613 lifetime users (multiple choice, % of 613): trying to calm the mind 257 (41.9%); changing location 168 (27.4%); asking for help from a friend 124 (20.2%); changing social environment 124 (20.2%); smoking cannabis 113 (18.4%); changing music 99 (16.2%); changing environment in another way 77 (12.6%); drinking alcohol 54 (8.8%); using the body to shift the experience 48 (7.8%); taking another drug 22 (3.6%).

anchors.locator: Results › Most Challenging, Difficult, or Distressing Experience, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: The five most commonly reported helpful interventions are named as calming the mind, changing location, asking a friend for help, changing social environment and smoking cannabis; changing music is sixth (16.2% against 18.4% for cannabis). Contradicts only the claim's 'fewer ticked' for cannabis.

anchors.locator: Materials and Methods › Measures › Most challenging, difficult, or distressing experience, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Every lifetime user recalled their most challenging experience and rated it on the 26-item CEQ (0-5, alpha .97); then, at the same sitting, ticked set-and-setting factors (list modified from Carbonaro et al., 2016), anything that helped in responding to or managing it (list derived from the same study), harm thoughts or attempts in the following days or weeks, help sought, and medications taken at the time.

anchors.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Calming the mind was the most common helpful intervention, said to correspond broadly with Carbonaro et al. (2016); the authors suggest introducing calming exercises such as mindfulness practice as preparation (a suggestion, not a tested finding).

anchors.locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph (limitations)
anchors.extracted: Cross-sectional design, so no causal inference; the panel was stratified on sex, age and ethnicity only; self-report measures open to bias.

claims.overstatement: None found for the Simonsson part. The claim narrows the abstract's 'nationally representative' to matching on sex, age and ethnicity only, flags that the attributed symptoms have no comparison, and calls the lithium and mood-stabilizer estimates too imprecise and confounded to give a risk. Two small points: 'glad' includes 'slightly agree' (142 of the 482); and the odds ratios are 'adjusted', as far as the text says, only for the other medication variables entered in the same model (Table 4 note; the Statistical Analyses paragraph names no covariates), not for age, sex or psychiatric history.
claims.note: Recomputed: 613/2822 = 21.7% (not printed in the paper). Never 362 (59.1%), rarely 143 (23.3%), occasionally 80 (13.1%), regularly 22 (3.6%) plus frequently 6 (1.0%) = 28 (4.6%); at least once 251/613 = 40.9%. Severe impairment 28 (4.6%). Impairment longer than a day 27 + 7 + 14 + 7 = 55 = 8.97% (the text prints 8.9%, the sum of rounded rows); over a month 14 + 7 = 21 = 3.4%. Some impairment (somewhat 98 + moderately 50 + severely 28) = 176, whereas 613 - 351 = 262 gave a length (207 of them one day or less): the mismatch is real. Harm thoughts or attempts 41 (6.7%), self-harm attempts 9 (1.5%), help sought 16 (2.6%). Symptoms 350 (57.1%), anxious 221 (36.1%), sleep 171 (27.9%). Glad 142 + 173 + 167 = 482 (78.6%). LSD 147 (24.0% of 613; 31.5% of lifetime LSD users), tryptamines 94 (15.3%; 19.7%), phenethylamines 25 (4.1%; 14.7%); the user denominators are only in Supplemental Table 1 (not read; implied about 467, 477 and 170). Lithium 8 (1.3%), other mood stabilizers 16 (2.6%). No item asked how often each drug was used (Measures list lifetime use only).

anchors.locator: Materials and Methods › Participants and Procedure, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: US residents aged 18 or over recruited on Prolific, 1-9 October 2021, N = 2,822, stratified by sex, five age bands and five ethnicity groups to mirror the US adult population; recruitment text did not mention psychedelics; 613 reported lifetime classic psychedelic use (21.7%, editors' calculation); paid $2.20.

anchors.extracted: Lifetime use = ever used ayahuasca, DMT, LSD, mescaline, peyote, San Pedro or psilocybin; no frequency of use item.

anchors.locator: Materials and Methods › Measures › Challenging, difficult, or distressing experiences, 1st paragraph and the gladness item that follows
anchors.extracted: Three items adapted from a population survey of meditation (Goldberg et al., 2021): frequency (never to frequently), impaired functioning (not applicable to severely), length of impairment (none to more than one year); which drug was associated (multiple choice); a modified 11-item meditation adverse-effects scale (MRAES-MBP) on enduring effects 'as a result of classic psychedelics', rated never to more than one year, also given to those who answered 'never'; gladness rated 1-6.

claims.overstatement: 'Blamed' renders the question whether the experience was 'associated with' each listed factor; as a description of a respondent's attribution it is fair. 'Later thoughts of harm' is narrower than the outcome, which was thoughts or attempts to hurt oneself or others (41 of 613); the odds ratio is for that composite.

reporting_issues.note: Found independently in step 1: every other row of Table 2 recomputes correctly.
Location: Materials and Methods › Participants and Procedure, 2nd paragraph, last sentence (the card gives no locator).

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E very high overall: no adjustment beyond mutual adjustment within each block, and exposure and outcome reported together about a recalled experience. The card rightly separates using the paper for the proportions in this sample from using it for predictors.

interpretation_gap.note: 'Substantial' is defensible: 'nationally representative' and 'covariate-adjusted' in the abstract, plus the Discussion's advice on guidelines, legalization and mindfulness preparation. Against that, the language is associational throughout and the limitations paragraph states the main caveats.

missed: Materials and Methods › Participants and Procedure, 1st paragraph: the sample size was planned from a published prevalence estimate (ref. 17), at about 395 people with lifetime use among about 2,800 respondents, which implies an expected 14.1% (editors' calculation). The panel gave 21.7%, about 1.5 times that, which points to the opt-in panel over-representing people who have used psychedelics (or to a rise in use). The card says the 21.7% was 'not compared with any national survey in the paper' and misses this comparison inside the paper.

Trivial, no consequence: Table 1 prints 8.7% for 53 people twice ('Other significant symptoms', 'Slightly disagree'), where 53 of 613 is 8.6% (apparently rounded twice); Table 2 prints '1,1' for other antipsychotic medications.
